content.content:
1	# ChronicleFlow
2	
3	ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
4	workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
5	SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.
6	
7	The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:
8	
9	- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, bounded
10	  `loop`, and dynamic `map` nodes;
11	- a workflow may declare named versions: every declared version is kept and
12	  each execution is bound to the version that was current (or explicitly
13	  named) when it started, so upgrading a workflow never changes a running
14	  execution, and a running execution can be explicitly migrated to another
15	  version of the same workflow, after which it advances under that version;
16	- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
17	  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
18	- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
19	  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
20	  execution;
21	- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
22	  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
23	  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
24	  execution with reason `rejected`);
25	- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
26	  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
27	- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
28	  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
29	- a map node inside a loop body expands independently in every iteration
30	  from that iteration's source output, its instances and events belonging
31	  to the iteration they expanded in;
32	- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
33	- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
34	- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
35	  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
36	  latest checkpoint after a restart;
37	- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
38	  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
39	  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
40	  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
41	- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
42	- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
43	  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
44	  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
45	- subscriptions may also declare queue targets instead of webhook addresses:
46	  matching business events are appended, in occurrence order, to persistent
47	  per-execution queues that callers pull from and acknowledge explicitly,
48	  with a visibility timeout returning unacknowledged messages to the pending
49	  set (delivery is at least once);
50	- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
51	  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
52	  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
53	  resumed, periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
54	  skipped, according to the declared missed policy, and a read-only preview
55	  query projects the upcoming trigger times and their inputs.
56	
57	## Requirements
58	
59	- Python 3.11 or newer
60	- no third-party runtime dependencies
61	
62	## Run the service
63	
64	```bash
65	PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
66	```
67	
68	The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
69	has bound the port.
70	
71	## HTTP API
72	
73	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
74	
75	Responses are compact JSON with no insignificant whitespace, and every
76	response body ends with exactly one trailing newline (`\n`). Numbers
77	round-trip with their full precision: finite floats keep their original
78	IEEE-754 value through the shortest textual representation that decodes to
79	it (so `0.30000000000000004` stays `0.30000000000000004`), negative zero is
80	preserved as `-0.0`, and integers stay integers. Non-finite numbers may
81	never appear in a request and are never produced in a response; timestamps
82	are ISO-8601 UTC strings ending in `Z`.
83	
84	### Tenants and quotas
85	
86	A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
87	non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
88	delivery history, and queue record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
89	created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
90	tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
91	identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
92	example advancing, migrating, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
93	reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, queues, or schedule of an execution or
94	workflow owned by another tenant, or pulling from or acknowledging one of its
95	queues — is answered exactly like a reference to a
96	missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
97	exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
98	workflow of the same tenant, and a migration can only name a version of that
99	workflow in the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier or
100	version is the usual `404 not_found`.
101	
102	The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
103	including creation, advancement, migration, approval decisions, lease
104	operations, cancellation, recovery, replay, instance deletion and
105	modification and re-expansion, queue pulls, acknowledgements, and all
106	history and status queries, as well as the quota declaration, the price
107	declaration and price delete, the price read, and the usage, bill, and
108	metrics queries. An empty
109	`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
110	header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
111	approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
112	scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
113	stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
114	and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
115	scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
116	other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
117	the usual `409 conflict`.
118	
119	A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
120	hold:
121	
122	```http
123	PUT /quotas
124	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
125	X-Tenant-Id: acme
126	
127	{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
128	```
129	
130	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
131	`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer; a non-positive,
132	non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
133	non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Both quota
134	routes require a tenant: calling them without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
135	one) is a `400 validation_error`. The response is
136	`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
137	limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
138	holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
139	fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.
140	
141	```http
142	GET /quotas
143	X-Tenant-Id: acme
144	```
145	
146	Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
147	when the tenant has declared none.
148	
149	When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the whole request is
150	rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
151	example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
152	10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
153	conflict. The rejection performs no partial write: nothing is inserted and
154	previously stored data is unaffected, exactly as for validation failures.
155	
156	A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
157	that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
158	is at its execution limit, the due period creates no execution and the
159	schedule is left unchanged — its cursor, `last_triggered_at`, and
160	`last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the period is settled on a later
161	pass once capacity exists, under the usual per-period idempotence. Delivery
162	history follows the tenant of the execution it belongs to.
163	
164	### Tenant price tables
165	
166	The bill's baseline unit prices are built in. A tenant may instead declare
167	its own price table on a separate entry point with the same calling shape as
168	the quota declaration:
169	
170	```http
171	PUT /prices
172	Idempotency-Key: price-request-1
173	X-Tenant-Id: acme
174	
175	{"execution_started":200,"workflow_created":1500}
176	```
177	
178	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must be a non-empty
179	JSON object giving a map of metered action type to a positive-integer unit
180	price in cents. A non-positive, non-integer, boolean, or non-finite price,
181	an unknown metered type, a missing field (an empty object), an extra field
182	that is not a metered type, or a non-object body is a `400
183	validation_error` that writes nothing. Every price route requires a tenant:
184	declaring, deleting, and reading without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
185	one) is a `400 validation_error`, and an unknown query parameter on the
186	read or the delete is rejected the same way, with the message naming the
187	offending parameter. The response is
188	`{"prices":{"execution_started":200,"workflow_created":1500}}`, with the
189	declared types in ascending type-identifier order.
190	
191	A successful declaration replaces the tenant's price table as a whole with
192	exactly the types given this time; metered types the declaration does not
193	name fall back to the built-in default prices when a bill is taken. The
194	declaration rewrites no recorded usage counts and changes no bill taken
195	before it was made.
196	
197	```http
198	GET /prices
199	X-Tenant-Id: acme
200	```
201	
202	Returns the price table currently declared by the tenant, in ascending
203	type-identifier order, or the definite empty result `{"prices":null}` for a
204	tenant that has never declared one. The stored table lists only the types
205	the declaration named; types left at the default are not copied into it.
206	
207	A tenant can also remove the table it declared, on the same path with the
208	`DELETE` method and the same calling shape as the other price writes:
209	
210	```http
211	DELETE /prices
212	Idempotency-Key: price-delete-1
213	X-Tenant-Id: acme
214	
215	{}
216	```
217	
218	The body must be exactly an empty object; a non-empty or non-object body,
219	an unknown field, or a non-finite value is a `400 validation_error` that
220	touches no price table. The delete removes the table as a whole and leaves
221	no partial write: it is atomic with the declaration and the read, so a
222	concurrent reader sees either the complete old table or no table at all.
223	After it succeeds the tenant no longer holds a declared table, and both the
224	delete response and the following read give the definite empty result
225	`{"prices":null}`. Deleting the table of a tenant that never declared one
226	returns that same definite empty result rather than an error. The delete
227	rewrites no recorded usage counts and changes no bill taken before it was
228	made; afterward both the bill and the bucketed bill price every type at the
229	built-in default, each line still giving the metered type, the actual
230	`unit_price` used, the `count`, and the integer-cent `subtotal`.
231	
232	The declaration and the delete follow the same idempotency rules as every
233	other write: the `Idempotency-Key` header is required, repeating the same
234	declaration or the same delete with the same key returns the first result
235	and performs no second replacement or removal, and reusing a key for
236	another operation — including another price declaration or a price delete
237	— in the same tenant is a `409 conflict` that leaves the tenant's price
238	table unchanged. Price tables are scoped per tenant like everything else: a
239	tenant can never read or delete another's declaration, and another tenant's
240	declaration or deletion never affects this tenant's bill amounts.
241	
242	The bill and the bucketed bill price with the price table in effect **at
243	query time**: a named type uses the tenant's declared price and every other
244	type uses the built-in default. Each returned line still gives the metered
245	type, the actual `unit_price` used, the `count`, and the integer-cent
246	`subtotal`, and the total is exactly the sum of the listed subtotals; types
247	with no matching record are still omitted rather than listed at zero. A
248	declaration affects only later queries — it neither rewrites recorded usage
249	nor revises historical bills — changes no metering, and leaves the bill and
250	usage queries read-only. A delete affects only later queries in the same
251	way: the table is removed as a whole, later bills fall back to the
252	built-in defaults, and recorded usage and already-taken bills stay exactly
253	as they were.
254	
255	### Usage metering and billing
256	
257	Requests that carry a tenant identifier leave a usage record for each billable
258	action they perform. Only tenant-scoped requests are metered: a request that
259	omits the `X-Tenant-Id` header keeps the legacy namespace and writes no usage
260	record at all, with its state shapes and event content unchanged. The four
261	metered action types are:
262	
263	- `workflow_created` — a workflow definition is stored. Adding a new version
264	  to an existing workflow is one workflow creation, the same as the first
265	  definition;
266	- `execution_started` — an execution is created and starts `running`;
267	- `schedule_triggered` — a due schedule period creates its execution. The
268	  scheduled execution is metered both as `execution_started` and as
269	  `schedule_triggered`;
270	- `delivery_attempted` — one outbound webhook HTTP attempt is made, or one
271	  queue message is delivered to a caller pulling from a queue. A
272	  subscription that retries is metered once per attempt, so a delivery that
273	  fails and then succeeds on its second attempt records two attempts; the
274	  action is metered whether it ultimately succeeds or fails. A queue pull
275	  meters one attempt per message it delivers, so a redelivery after the
276	  visibility timeout is metered again, while a pull that delivers nothing
277	  meters nothing.
278	
279	Metering is atomic with the action it describes: a write rejected by
280	validation or by a quota produces no record and performs no partial write.
281	Repeating an idempotent command returns its first result and writes no second
282	record, and settling the same schedule period more than once (a repeated
283	trigger or a later pass) meters that period only once. Replay, recovery, and
284	queries never meter and never alter recorded usage or billing conclusions.
285	
286	```http
287	GET /usage
288	X-Tenant-Id: acme
289	```
290	
291	Returns `{"usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}`: the
292	cumulative count of recorded actions per type, sorted by ascending type
293	identifier. Types with no records are omitted, so a tenant with no usage gets
294	the definite empty result `{"usage":[]}`.
295	
296	```http
297	GET /bill
298	X-Tenant-Id: acme
299	```
300	
301	Returns the per-type bill:
302	
303	```json
304	{"bill":{"items":[
305	  {"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100},
306	  {"type":"workflow_created","count":2,"unit_price":1000,"subtotal":2000}
307	],"total":2100}}
308	```
309	
310	Each item gives the metered `count`, a positive-integer `unit_price` in cents
311	that is also returned in the response, and a `subtotal` equal to
312	`count * unit_price`; `total` is the integer-cent sum of every subtotal. With
313	no records, `items` is empty and `total` is `0`. The price used per type is
314	the tenant's declared price when its price table names that type and the
315	built-in default otherwise, read from the table in effect at query time (see
316	[Tenant price tables](#tenant-price-tables)); tenants with no declaration are
317	billed byte for byte as before.
318	
319	Both endpoints accept the same optional query parameters the events and
320	metrics queries accept: an optional metered-type filter and an ISO-8601 UTC
321	timestamp window, each timestamp ending in `Z`, plus an optional fixed time
322	bucket:
323	
324	```http
325	GET /usage?type=execution_started,workflow_created&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
326	GET /bill?type=execution_started&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
327	X-Tenant-Id: acme
328	```
329	
330	- `type` names one metered action type or a comma-separated set of them; only
331	  records whose type is in the set are counted. A single identifier needs no
332	  comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown metered type is a
333	  `400 validation_error`; when `type` is absent every type is counted, exactly
334	  as before;
335	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on each usage record's
336	  occurrence time: a record whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted.
337	  When either parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting
338	  both returns exactly the cumulative result above;
339	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
340	  parameter is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing;
341	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
342	  simply contains no records. Usage then reports the definite empty result
343	  `{"usage":[]}`, and the bill reports an empty `items` list with a `total` of
344	  `0`.
345	
346	The type filter and the time window apply together as an intersection: a
347	record is counted only when its type is named **and** its occurrence time is
348	in the window. A type the filter names but that has no matching record is
349	omitted rather than reported at zero, so a filter that matches nothing gives
350	the same definite empty results as an empty window: `{"usage":[]}` for usage
351	and an empty `items` list with a `total` of `0` for the bill.
352	
353	Both endpoints also accept an optional `bucket` parameter for a fixed-bucket
354	trend summary, so callers never have to pull records and group them
355	themselves:
356	
357	```http
358	GET /usage?bucket=hour&since=2026-09-26T00:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-27T00:00:00.000Z
359	GET /bill?bucket=day&type=execution_started
360	X-Tenant-Id: acme
361	```
362	
363	- `bucket` is exactly `hour` or `day`: `hour` buckets start on the UTC hour
364	  and `day` buckets at UTC midnight, both aligned solely to UTC. An empty or
365	  any other value is a `400 validation_error`, exactly like a repeated
366	  parameter or an unknown query parameter;
367	- when `bucket` is present, usage returns
368	  `{"usage_buckets":[{"bucket_start":"2026-09-26T08:00:00Z","usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}, ...]}`:
369	  the buckets with at least one matching record, in ascending bucket-start
370	  order. Each entry gives its `bucket_start` first — an ISO-8601 UTC string
371	  ending in `Z` at the hour or midnight — followed by `usage`, the per-type
372	  counts inside that bucket in ascending type-identifier order; a type with no
373	  record in the bucket is omitted;
374	- when `bucket` is present, the bill returns
375	  `{"bill":{"buckets":[{"bucket_start":"2026-09-26T00:00:00Z","items":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100}, ...],"subtotal":100}, ...],"total":100}}`.
376	  Buckets appear in ascending bucket-start order; each bucket's `items` stay
377	  sorted by ascending type identifier, each line giving the filtered count,
378	  the usual positive-integer `unit_price`, and an integer-cent `subtotal` of
379	  the two, and a type with no matching record is omitted rather than reported
380	  at zero. Each bucket also carries its own `subtotal`, and the window
381	  `total` is exactly the sum of the listed per-bucket subtotals, all amounts
382	  integer cents;
383	- a bucket that holds no matching record never appears, so an empty tenant, a
384	  window with `since` later than `until`, or a filter that matches nothing
385	  returns the definite empty bucket lists `{"usage_buckets":[]}` and
386	  `{"bill":{"buckets":[],"total":0}` — never an error, with the empty bill's
387	  total at `0`;
388	- bucketing applies together with the type filter and the time window as an
389	  intersection: a bucket holds only records whose occurrence time is in the
390	  closed window **and** whose type the filter names. The window keeps its
391	  closed endpoints, its open bounds when either side is omitted, and the
392	  existing rule for when a record's instant falls in it; buckets are simply
393	  the same matching records rolled up to their UTC bucket;
394	- the bucketed queries are read-only like the others: they append no usage
395	  records, change no metering basis or prices, and never alter recorded usage
396	  or billing conclusions — under event replay or recovery the same window,
397	  type filter, and bucket always give the same answer;
398	- omitting `bucket` leaves both queries exactly as before: the same compact
399	  JSON responses with `usage` / `items` shapes, full float precision and the
400	  `-0.0` convention, byte for byte. The parameter introduces no second
401	  protocol and changes no entry point's existing behavior.
402	
403	Only records whose occurrence time falls in the window are counted. Within
404	the window the bill keeps the same basis as always: each present type reports
405	its filtered, windowed count, its usual `unit_price`, and a `subtotal` of the
406	two; items stay sorted by ascending type identifier, and a type with no
407	matching record is omitted rather than reported at zero. The bill's `total`
408	is exactly the sum of the subtotals of the listed items. The query is
409	read-only: it writes no usage records, changes no prices or metering
410	conclusions, and never alters already recorded usage — under event replay or
411	recovery the same window and type filter always give the same answer.
412	
413	Both endpoints are tenant-scoped `GET` requests: a missing or empty
414	`X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error` that reveals no usage. Usage and
415	bill data follow the usual tenant isolation, so one tenant can never see
416	another's records under any type filter or window, and another tenant's
417	records never affect this tenant's counts or totals.
418	
419	### Per-record usage history
420	
421	The cumulative usage query reports only per-type totals. A separate endpoint
422	returns the individual usage records themselves, so each billed action can be
423	checked against the moment it occurred:
424	
425	```http
426	GET /usage/records?limit=50
427	X-Tenant-Id: acme
428	```
429	
430	Returns `{"records":[...]}` with the matching records in ascending order of
431	occurrence time; records sharing one instant are ordered by ascending
432	sequence. Each record is:
433	
434	```json
435	{"sequence":7,"type":"execution_started","occurred_at":"2026-09-26T08:30:00.000Z"}
436	```
437	
438	- `sequence` is a stable, strictly increasing positive integer per tenant. It
439	  identifies the record across every query and is never renumbered by a
440	  filter or a page;
441	- `type` is the metered action type;
442	- `occurred_at` is the record's occurrence time as an ISO-8601 UTC string
443	  ending in `Z`.
444	
445	A tenant with no matching records gets the definite empty result
446	`{"records":[]}`, never an error. The response ends with a single newline,
447	like every other JSON endpoint.
448	
449	The endpoint accepts an optional metered-type filter, the same optional
450	closed time window the events and usage queries accept, plus cursor
451	pagination:
452	
453	```http
454	GET /usage/records?type=execution_started,workflow_created&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
455	```
456	
457	- `type` names one metered action type or a comma-separated set of them;
458	  only records whose type is in the set are returned. A single identifier
459	  needs no comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown metered
460	  type is a `400 validation_error`; when `type` is absent every type is
461	  returned, exactly as before;
462	- `since` and `until` are ISO-8601 UTC timestamps ending in `Z` and bind a
463	  **closed** interval on each record's occurrence time: a record whose time
464	  equals either boundary is included. When either is absent the corresponding
465	  bound is open; when `since` is later than `until` the window matches
466	  nothing and the definite empty list is returned;
467	- `limit` is **required** and must be a positive integer; a page never
468	  contains more than that many records;
469	- `cursor` is the `sequence` of the previous page's last record; only records
470	  whose `sequence` is strictly greater are returned, so pages neither overlap
471	  nor skip. It is omitted on the first page and must be a positive integer;
472	- the type filter, time window, and pagination apply together as an
473	  intersection, and filtering never changes a record's `sequence`.
474	
475	A malformed timestamp, an unknown, empty, or duplicated `type` entry, a
476	missing or non-positive-integer `limit`, a non-positive-integer `cursor`, a
477	repeated parameter, or any unknown query parameter is a `400
478	validation_error` that writes nothing. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a
479	`400 validation_error` that reveals no records. The query is read-only: it
480	appends no usage records, writes no events, and changes no metering, prices,
481	quotas, or billing conclusions. Records follow the usual tenant isolation, so
482	another tenant's records are never visible under any type filter, window, or
483	page and never affect this tenant's result; replay and recovery leave every
484	recorded sequence, time, and billing conclusion unchanged.
485	
486	### Operational metrics
487	
488	```http
489	GET /metrics
490	X-Tenant-Id: acme
491	```
492	
493	Returns one line of compact JSON summarizing the business facts already
494	recorded for the tenant, ending with the usual single newline. The endpoint
495	is read-only: it appends no events, writes no usage records, and changes no
496	stored data, and it reports only persisted facts — it performs no
497	advancement, approval, recovery, or replay of its own, so those operations
498	never change what a metrics query observes beyond the facts they themselves
499	recorded. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`, and
500	the metrics follow the usual tenant isolation: another tenant's facts are
501	never visible in any dimension and never affect this tenant's counts. A
502	tenant with no recorded facts at all gets the definite empty result with
503	every dimension at zero — not an error. With no query parameters the answer
504	is every fact recorded for the tenant, byte for byte.
505	
506	The query accepts two optional query parameters, each an ISO-8601 UTC
507	timestamp ending in `Z`:
508	
509	```http
510	GET /metrics?since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
511	X-Tenant-Id: acme
512	```
513	
514	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on the facts' occurrence
515	  times: a fact whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted. When either
516	  parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting both
517	  counts every recorded fact;
518	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
519	  parameter is a `400 validation_error`;
520	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
521	  simply contains no facts, so every dimension reports its definite zero
522	  result.
523	
524	Each dimension is windowed by the occurrence time of its own fact: node
525	completions, failures, and retry consumption use the time of their recorded
526	node events; delivery outcomes use the delivery record's `occurred_at`
527	(shared by every attempt recorded in it); schedule triggers use the settled
528	period's trigger time; and the status distribution counts an execution at
529	the time it entered its current status — a still-running execution at its
530	start time, and a completed or terminated execution at the time of its
531	completion or termination event.
532	
533	### Export metrics in Prometheus text format
534	
535	```http
536	GET /metrics/export
537	X-Tenant-Id: acme
538	```
539	
540	A read-only tenant-scoped entry point that returns the same counts as the
541	metrics query — including the same optional `since` and `until` filters, the
542	same closed-interval semantics, the same definite zero result for a window
543	with `since` later than `until`, and the same `400 validation_error` for a
544	missing or empty tenant, a malformed timestamp, or an unknown query
545	parameter — rendered in the Prometheus text exposition format
546	(`text/plain; version=0.0.4`). It writes no events and no usage records.
547	
548	Each top-level metrics dimension is one metric family named with the
549	dimension's public key prefixed by `chronicleflow_`. The families appear in
550	the documented top-level key order, and the samples within a family are
551	ordered by ascending label value:
552	
553	- `chronicleflow_status_distribution` — samples carry a `status` label
554	  (`running`, `completed`, `terminated`); only the terminated samples also
555	  carry a `reason` label naming one of the four termination reasons;
556	- `chronicleflow_node_completions`, `chronicleflow_node_failures`, and
557	  `chronicleflow_retry_consumption` — samples carry a `node` label;
558	- `chronicleflow_schedule_triggers` — samples carry a `workflow` label;
559	- `chronicleflow_delivery_succeeded` and `chronicleflow_delivery_failed` —
560	  unlabeled scalar samples.
561	
562	Every value is a decimal integer. A dimension with no facts in the window
563	still exposes a zero-valued sample line (the labeled families expose one
564	unlabeled `0` sample). Every line ends with a newline and the whole document
565	ends with a single newline.
566	
567	The top-level keys appear in this order — status distribution, node
568	completions, node failures, retry consumption, delivery successes, delivery
569	failures, and schedule triggers:
570	
571	```json
572	{"status_distribution":{"running":1,"completed":2,"terminated":{"cancelled":0,"rejected":1,"retries_exhausted":0,"timeout":0}},"node_completions":{"charge":3},"node_failures":{"charge":2},"retry_consumption":{"charge":1},"delivery_succeeded":4,"delivery_failed":1,"schedule_triggers":{"nightly-orders":2}}
573	```
574	
575	- `status_distribution` — the tenant's executions divided into `running`,
576	  `completed`, and `terminated`; `terminated` is further broken down by
577	  termination reason, with every reason (`cancelled`, `rejected`,
578	  `retries_exhausted`, `timeout`) always present, zero when no execution
579	  ended for that reason.
580	- `node_completions` — persisted node completion facts per node identifier.
581	  Condition evaluations and skips are not completions and are never counted;
582	  a loop body node counts once per iteration it completes.
583	- `node_failures` — submitted task failures per node identifier; a loop body
584	  node accumulates each iteration's failures.
585	- `retry_consumption` — the number of times a failed task was re-queued for
586	  another attempt, per node identifier.
587	- `delivery_succeeded` and `delivery_failed` — outbound delivery attempts by
588	  outcome. Every attempt counts exactly once, so a delivery that fails and
589	  then succeeds on a later attempt records one of each.
590	- `schedule_triggers` — schedule periods that created an execution, per
591	  workflow identifier; settling the same period again counts nothing more.
592	
593	All counts are non-negative integers. A dimension with no facts reports zero
594	(or an empty group) rather than being omitted, and the groups within a
595	dimension are ordered by ascending identifier. Migrating an execution to
596	another version does not change attribution: facts recorded before and after
597	the migration accumulate under the same names. The optional `since` and
598	`until` filters and the Prometheus text export are described above.
599	
600	### Health
601	
602	```http
603	GET /health
604	```
605	
606	Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.
607	
608	### Create a workflow
609	
610	```http
611	POST /workflows
612	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
613	
614	{
615	  "id": "order-flow",
616	  "nodes": [
617	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
618	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
619	  ]
620	}
621	```
622	
623	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
624	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
625	
626	A workflow definition may carry an optional `version` tag; declaring one
627	enables upgrades and keeps every version. Versioning is described under
628	"Workflow versions" below, and a workflow's stored versions and current
629	version are available through `GET /workflows/{id}`.
630	
631	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
632	
633	```json
634	{
635	  "id": "order-flow",
636	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
637	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
638	}
639	```
640	
641	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
642	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow (for a
643	versioned workflow, to executions bound to that version).
644	
645	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
646	
647	```json
648	{
649	  "id": "nightly-orders",
650	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
651	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
652	}
653	```
654	
655	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
656	
657	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
658	
659	```json
660	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
661	```
662	
663	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
664	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
665	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
666	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
667	`false`.
668	
669	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
670	
671	```json
672	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
673	```
674	
675	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
676	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
677	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
678	dependencies of its successors.
679	
680	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
681	
682	```json
683	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
684	```
685	
686	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
687	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
688	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
689	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
690	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
691	`retries_exhausted`.
692	
693	A task may instead declare an approval point:
694	
695	```json
696	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
697	```
698	
699	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
700	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
701	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
702	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
703	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
704	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
705	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
706	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
707	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
708	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
709	move the task.
710	
711	### Submit an approval decision
712	
713	```http
714	POST /executions/run-1/decision
715	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
716	
717	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
718	```
719	
720	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
721	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
722	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
723	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
724	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
725	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
726	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
727	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
728	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
729	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
730	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
731	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
732	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
733	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
734	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
735	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
736	404.
737	
738	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
739	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
740	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
741	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
742	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
743	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
744	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
745	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
746	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
747	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
748	shape and event stream.
749	
750	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
751	segment:
752	
753	```json
754	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
755	```
756	
757	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
758	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
759	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
760	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the repeated segment anchored by
761	the entry task and the condition: it is the entry task, the condition, and
762	every node either anchor reaches through `depends_on`. The two anchors must
763	be connected — the condition gates the entry task (the entry depends on it)
764	or the condition is evaluated after the entry task (it depends on the entry),
765	as in the example above. The body keeps the usual DAG rules and always
766	contains the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
767	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
768	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
769	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
770	loop node instead).
771	
772	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
773	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
774	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
775	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
776	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
777	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
778	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
779	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
780	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
781	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
782	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
783	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors. Once the loop
784	has finished, the execution-level `completed_nodes` list also includes every
785	body node that completed in any iteration, each listed only once and in the
786	order of its first completion, followed by the loop node itself; body nodes
787	skipped by a `run_if` guard remain out of the execution-level completed list
788	and are visible only in their iteration record. Body task outputs still
789	belong only to their iterations.
790	
791	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
792	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
793	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
794	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
795	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
796	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
797	exactly.
798	
799	### Dynamic map nodes
800	
801	A `map` node expands at runtime into one task instance per element of a
802	recorded array:
803	
804	```json
805	{"id": "ship", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["collect"],
806	 "source": "collect", "path": "items", "max_instances": 100,
807	 "template": {"id": "ship-item", "retries": 2}}
808	```
809	
810	A map node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `source`, `path`,
811	`max_instances`, and `template`; any other field is rejected as unknown.
812	
813	- `source` names a `task` node that is also listed in `depends_on`. Expansion
814	  begins only after every dependency has completed or been skipped; the
815	  element list comes solely from the source task's recorded output.
816	- `path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into that recorded output, using
817	  the same path syntax as a condition.
818	- `max_instances` is a positive integer bounding how many elements may
819	  expand.
820	- `template` describes the single task each instance runs and contains
821	  exactly an `id`, and optionally `retries` (an integer between 0 and 10,
822	  defaulting to 0) and an `approval` point with the same shape a task node
823	  uses. The template id only names the dynamically expanded instances; it
824	  may coincide with a declared node id or with another map's template id.
825	  A map node may also sit inside a loop body, expanding independently in
826	  every iteration (see "Maps inside loop bodies" below).
827	
828	When the dependencies settle, the value at `path` is read once. When it is an
829	array, one instance is created per element; the instances queue in ascending
830	element index order. Each `advance` still settles exactly one ready item, so
831	instances are worked in index order, one per call. An instance is an ordinary
832	task in every other respect: a submitted failure consumes the template's
833	retry bound and re-queues that instance, and a template approval point parks
834	the execution with the instance's `map_id` and `index` recorded, until an
835	approver decides it. Retries and approvals are per instance: results never
836	overwrite another instance.
837	
838	When every instance is completed, the map node completes and its output,
839	recorded both in the node's `outputs` entry and under its `maps` record, is
840	the list of instance outputs in ascending element order; its successors then
841	become available in the usual way.
842	
843	A value that is missing or is not an array expands to zero instances: the map
844	completes with an empty output list and releases its successors immediately.
845	When the array holds more elements than `max_instances`, no instance is
846	created at all: the map node fails permanently, is listed under
847	`failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`
848	under the usual exhaustion semantics.
849	
850	Execution state exposes each map under `maps`: the node's `status`
851	(`pending`, `running`, `completed`, or `failed`), one record per retained
852	instance giving its `index`, `status` (`ready`, `waiting`, `completed`, or
853	`failed`), its `output`, and its `failure_reason` (null except for a
854	permanently failed instance), plus the ordered completed `outputs` list and
855	the node's single `failure_reason`. A `ready` instance that has been
856	rewritten by a successful modify additionally carries that rewritten
857	`input`; every other instance record keeps exactly these fields. The `maps`
858	field is present only when the bound workflow declares a map node outside
859	any loop body; every other execution keeps its previous state shape.
860	
861	The event stream records a `map_expanded` event when expansion happens,
862	carrying the map id and the number of created instances (zero for a missing
863	or non-array value, and zero together with `exceeded` and the observed
864	element count when the bound is exceeded), and a `map_completed` event with
865	the map id and final instance count. Each instance's per-node events —
866	`node_completed`, `node_failed`, and `node_retried`, plus
867	`approval_requested` and `approval_decided` for a template approval point —
868	carry their `map_id` and element `index` alongside the template node id, so
869	replay rebuilds every instance solely from the event stream. Checkpoints are
870	written at instance boundaries, so recovery resumes with the unfinished
871	instances and never repeats an instance output. Per-instance completions and
872	failures count toward the existing node metrics under the template node id,
873	and webhook and queue subscriptions receive instance events exactly like any
874	other node event. Instance deletion and modification add their own
875	`instance_deleted` and `instance_modified` events, and re-expansion adds a
876	`map_reexpanded` event, described under
877	"Delete and modify expanded instances" below.
878	
879	### Maps inside loop bodies
880	
881	A map node may belong to a loop body — it is part of the body exactly when
882	the loop's entry or condition reaches it through `depends_on`, like any
883	other body member:
884	
885	```json
886	{"id": "fanout", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["attempt"],
887	 "source": "attempt", "path": "items", "max_instances": 10,
888	 "template": {"id": "work", "retries": 1}}
889	```
890	
891	A nested map expands once per iteration, when every dependency of its node
892	is completed or skipped in that iteration, and the element list is read from
893	the source task's output of that same iteration. The expansion rules are the
894	ones of an execution-level map: a missing path or a non-array value expands
895	to zero instances and the map completes for that iteration with an empty
896	output list, so the loop boundary is evaluated as usual; an element count
897	beyond `max_instances` creates no instance at all — the map fails
898	permanently, is listed under `failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates
899	with reason `retries_exhausted` under the usual exhaustion semantics.
900	
901	The expanded instances belong to their iteration only: they queue in
902	ascending element index order and are settled one per `advance`, exactly
903	like execution-level instances, and one iteration's instances never
904	overwrite another iteration's results. An instance is an ordinary task in
905	every other respect — a submitted failure consumes the template's retry
906	bound and re-queues that instance within its iteration, and a template
907	approval point parks the execution until an approver decides it — with no
908	influence from the iteration number.
909	
910	Iteration state exposes each nested map under the iteration record's `maps`
911	field, with the same per-map shape as an execution-level map (`status`, one
912	record per instance, the ordered completed `outputs`, and `failure_reason`);
913	the field is present on every iteration of a loop whose body declares a map
914	node. When a nested map completes, its node enters the iteration's
915	`completed_nodes` and its output list is recorded in the iteration's
916	`outputs`; when the loop finishes, the usual roll-up lists the map node once
917	in the execution-level `completed_nodes`, while its outputs stay with their
918	iterations. An execution-level `maps` field is not created for nested maps.
919	
920	Every event a nested expansion records carries the owning `loop_id` and
921	`iteration` alongside the map id and, for per-instance events, the element
922	`index`: `map_expanded`, `map_completed`, the per-instance `node_completed`,
923	`node_failed`, and `node_retried`, and `approval_requested` and
924	`approval_decided` for a template approval point. The `iteration_started`
925	event of a loop whose body declares map nodes carries the iteration's
926	initial `maps` skeleton, so replay rebuilds every iteration's instance list,
927	status, and ownership solely from the event stream, consistent with the
928	materialized state. Checkpoints are written at each iteration's instance
929	boundaries, so recovery continues the current iteration's unfinished
930	instances and never repeats an instance output. Cancellation, timeouts,
931	leases, retries, and approvals keep their existing semantics, and a nested
932	map never changes an execution's termination reason.
933	
934	Executions whose workflows declare no nested map behave exactly as before:
935	state fields, event contents, and advancement results are unchanged.
936	
937	### Delete and modify expanded instances
938	
939	An expanded dynamic node offers, alongside expansion and per-instance
940	advancement, two instance-level operations and a node-level re-expansion.
941	All three are ordinary idempotent HTTP commands over the same entry points
942	the rest of the service uses; they introduce no second protocol.
943	
944	An instance that has never advanced can be removed, and so can an instance
945	that has permanently failed:
946	
947	```http
948	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/2/delete
949	Idempotency-Key: delete-instance-2
950	
951	{}
952	```
953	
954	The body must be an empty object. Removing an instance drops only that
955	instance's record: every retained instance keeps its element index, its
956	place in the queue, and its advancement order. When the removed instance was
957	the map's last unfinished instance, the node completes under the existing
958	rules with an output list containing only the retained instances' outputs,
959	in ascending element-index order, and its successors unlock as usual. An
960	instance that is waiting on an approval, or has already completed, can never
961	be deleted; attempting it returns `409 conflict` and changes no state. A
962	permanently failed instance is removable after the execution has terminated,
963	but removing it never revives the execution, alters its termination reason,
964	or changes the node's failed conclusion. When every retained instance of a
965	map inside a loop body has ended, the iteration's other nodes advance as
966	usual and the node completes or ends under the existing rules; deleting an
967	instance in one iteration never touches another iteration.
968	
969	An instance that has never advanced can also have its input rewritten
970	before it is worked:
971	
972	```http
973	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/1/modify
974	Idempotency-Key: modify-instance-1
975	
976	{"input":{"address":"742 Evergreen Terrace"}}
977	```
978	
979	The body must contain exactly `input`, an object with the new content; it is
980	validated like every other request body (finite numbers only). The rewrite
981	changes only the parameters used when that one instance is later advanced:
982	it affects no other instance, and the output and history of an instance that
983	has already advanced (waiting, completed, or permanently failed) are
984	immutable — modifying such an instance returns `409 conflict` and changes no
985	state. The rewritten input, including its full float precision and `-0.0`,
986	is stored verbatim.
987	
988	Delete and modify calls on the same instance settle in call order: every
989	call applies to the instance list exactly as the earlier calls left it, and
990	several calls on one instance each take effect independently, one after
991	another. A rewritten instance has still never advanced, so it remains
992	deletable; deleting or modifying an instance an earlier call already
993	removed is a `404 not_found`; and a second rewrite of the same instance
994	records the first rewrite's content as its `before`.
995	
996	Both commands apply to a map nested in a loop body exactly as to an
997	execution-level map: the current running iteration's instances are
998	addressed by the same path, and every event they append carries the owning
999	`loop_id` and `iteration` alongside the map id; an execution-level instance
1000	carries no loop context.
1001	
1002	An out-of-bounds element index, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic
1003	`map`, a missing execution, or a cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found`
1004	and writes nothing. A missing or mistyped field, a non-object modify
1005	`input`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a `400 validation_error`
1006	with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a
1007	`409 conflict`; repeating the same command with the same key returns the
1008	first result and appends no second event.
1009	
1010	Every successful call appends exactly one event to the execution stream:
1011	
1012	- an `instance_deleted` event records the action type, the owning dynamic
1013	  node under `map_id`, the removed instance's element `index` and `status`
1014	  (`ready` or `failed`), and, for a map inside a loop body, the `loop_id`
1015	  and `iteration`;
1016	- an `instance_modified` event records the action type, the owning
1017	  `map_id`, the instance `index`, the content `before` the rewrite (`null`
1018	  for an instance that had never been rewritten) and `after` it, and the
1019	  same loop context when the instance belongs to an iteration.
1020	
1021	Replay rebuilds the instance list, every instance's status and ownership,
1022	and each rewrite solely from the event stream: a delete drops the recorded
1023	instance (and the subsequent `map_completed`, when the deletion finished the
1024	node, completes it with the retained outputs), and a modify applies the
1025	rewritten input to that one instance, so the rebuilt state is exactly the
1026	materialized state. A checkpoint is written at the instance boundary of
1027	every successful delete or modify; after a restart recovery continues the
1028	unfinished instances, repeats no instance output, and never resurrects a
1029	deleted instance. The operations change no advancement conclusion or
1030	termination semantics: cancellation, timeouts, approvals, leases, retries,
1031	and retry exhaustion keep their existing behavior. Executions that never
1032	use deletion, modification, or re-expansion keep exactly their current
1033	state fields, event contents, and advancement results.
1034	
1035	### Re-expand a dynamic node
1036	
1037	A dynamic node that has already expanded can be expanded again on demand —
1038	above all to regenerate its instance list after deletions:
1039	
1040	```http
1041	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/reexpand
1042	Idempotency-Key: reexpand-1
1043	
1044	{}
1045	```
1046	
1047	(The same operation is also accepted at `.../maps/ship/expand`.) The body
1048	must be an empty object. Re-expansion reads the element list again from the
1049	source task's recorded output — the same recorded output the first
1050	expansion read, which never changes once recorded — and regenerates the
1051	instance list from it: every previous instance record is replaced, and the
1052	fresh instances queue from element index zero in ascending order. The
1053	regenerated instances are ordinary instances in every respect: they are
1054	deleted, modified, advanced, retried, and approved through the same entries
1055	and with exactly the same behavior as a first expansion, and their retry
1056	bounds start from zero.
1057	
1058	Every successful call appends exactly one `map_reexpanded` event, recording
1059	the action type, the owning dynamic node under `map_id`, and the number of
1060	generated instances under `instance_count`; for a map inside a loop body
1061	the event also carries the owning `loop_id` and `iteration`, and only the
1062	current running iteration's expansion is replaced. A node that had
1063	completed returns to `running`: it leaves `completed_nodes`, its recorded
1064	output entry is discarded, and when the regenerated instances have all
1065	completed the node completes again under the existing rules, its result
1066	list holding only the finally retained instances' outputs in ascending
1067	element-index order. An empty element list completes the node again at
1068	once with an empty output list, exactly like a zero-element first
1069	expansion.
1070	
1071	Re-expansion is rejected with `409 conflict` and writes nothing when the
1072	node has not expanded yet, when it has permanently failed, when one of its
1073	instances is waiting on an approval decision, when the execution has
1074	already completed, or when a nested map's loop is not currently running.
1075	A terminated execution's unfinished node may still be re-expanded; doing so
1076	never revives the execution or alters its termination reason. A missing
1077	execution, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic `map`, or a
1078	cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found` and writes nothing. A
1079	non-empty or non-object body, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
1080	`400 validation_error` with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key
1081	from another operation is a `409 conflict`; repeating the same call with
1082	the same key returns the first result and appends no second event. Replay
1083	rebuilds the regenerated instance list, statuses, and ownership solely
1084	from the event stream, a checkpoint is written at the re-expansion
1085	boundary, and recovery after a restart continues the unfinished
1086	regenerated instances — repeating no instance output and never resurrecting
1087	an instance that stayed deleted.
1088	
1089	### Workflow versions
1090	
1091	A workflow can declare a version tag alongside its nodes:
1092	
1093	```json
1094	{
1095	  "id": "order-flow",
1096	  "version": "2026-09-25",
1097	  "nodes": [
1098	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
1099	    {"id": "ship", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
1100	  ]
1101	}
1102	```
1103	
1104	`version` is an optional non-empty string of at most 100 characters, validated
1105	like every other identifier. Posting it when the workflow does not yet exist
1106	creates the workflow with that version; posting another definition with a new
1107	`version` to the same `id` adds a new version without touching the previous
1108	ones — the workflow keeps its entire history, and every stored version remains
1109	usable. The most recently added version becomes the workflow's current
1110	version. Posting a definition without a `version` to an existing workflow
1111	still conflicts, and reusing a version tag already stored for the same
1112	workflow is a `409 conflict`; either rejection writes nothing.
1113	
1114	A version declaration may also carry `subscriptions` and a `schedule`,
1115	validated exactly like at creation. Subscriptions are attached to the
1116	declared version and apply only to executions bound to it; a version without
1117	subscriptions replaces none, and other versions' subscriptions stay intact.
1118	Declaring a `schedule` on an added version replaces the workflow's single
1119	schedule plan in the usual way (re-anchored, pause flag kept).
1120	
1121	An execution created without an explicit `version` binds to the workflow's
1122	current version at the moment it starts:
1123	
1124	```http
1125	POST /executions
1126	Idempotency-Key: execution-versioned
1127	
1128	{"id":"run-v2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{}}
1129	```
1130	
1131	An execution may instead name the version it wants:
1132	
1133	```json
1134	{"id":"run-v1","workflow_id":"order-flow","version":"2026-08-01","input":{}}
1135	```
1136	
1137	Naming a version that does not exist for the workflow is a missing-resource
1138	`404 not_found`, exactly like naming a workflow that does not exist; the
1139	execution is not created. Everything about an execution follows its bound
1140	version: ready-node selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval
1141	points, retry counts, leases, and the subscriptions that fire for its events.
1142	Adding a new version never interrupts an execution already running: an
1143	execution started before the upgrade keeps advancing on its old version to
1144	completion or termination. Its checkpoints are snapshots of the same state,
1145	recovery rebuilds from the bound version, and replay rebuilds state and the
1146	version binding solely from its event stream; recorded events and historical
1147	conclusions never change.
1148	
1149	A versioned execution's state carries its `version` tag, and its
1150	`execution_started` event records the same tag; querying it therefore shows
1151	which version it is bound to. A workflow that never declares a version, and an
1152	execution of one, keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
1153	stream with no added field.
1154	
1155	The definition query lists every version and the current one:
1156	
1157	```http
1158	GET /workflows/order-flow
1159	```
1160	
1161	```json
1162	{"current_version":"2026-09-25","id":"order-flow","versions":[
1163	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-08-01"},
1164	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-09-25"}
1165	]}
1166	```
1167	
1168	Versions are returned in declaration order; each entry is the stored
1169	definition with its `version` tag. A workflow that never declared a version
1170	returns a single untagged entry and `current_version: null`. A missing
1171	workflow returns 404 `not_found`. Cross-tenant references are missing
1172	resources as usual.
1173	
1174	### Migrate a running execution to another version
1175	
1176	```http
1177	POST /executions/run-v1/migrate
1178	Idempotency-Key: migrate-request-1
1179	
1180	{"version":"2026-09-25"}
1181	```
1182	
1183	A running execution can be explicitly moved to another declared version of
1184	the same workflow; after the call it keeps advancing under the new version.
1185	The body must contain exactly `version`, a non-empty version identifier that
1186	names a stored version of the execution's workflow. On success a
1187	`version_migrated` event is appended to the event stream — it records the
1188	`from_version`, the `to_version`, and the structural skeleton of the target
1189	revision (its `loops`, and, when it declares approval points, its
1190	`waiting_approval` and `approvals` fields) — and a checkpoint of the rebound
1191	state is written at that same node boundary. The execution's state then
1192	carries the target version.
1193	
1194	Everything that follows uses the target version's definition: ready-node
1195	selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval points, retries, and
1196	the workflow subscriptions that fire for later events. Everything recorded
1197	before the migration is kept exactly as-is: prior events, node outputs,
1198	condition conclusions, and per-iteration history are never rewritten. Loops
1199	introduced by the target definition begin in their initial pending state; a
1200	loop the old definition knew keeps its recorded iterations and conclusion.
1201	Replay rebuilds the migration point and version binding solely from the
1202	event stream, and after a restart recovery continues on the migrated version
1203	from the migration checkpoint, so checkpoints and materialized state agree.
1204	
1205	An execution parked at an approval point may also be migrated: the waiting
1206	point keeps its recorded node and approver list unchanged (only a recorded
1207	approver may still decide it), and once the decision lands the subsequent
1208	advancement follows the target version. Executions that are never migrated
1209	keep advancing on the version they started with to completion or
1210	termination; adding versions never moves them. An execution of a workflow
1211	that never declared a version cannot name a target, and such workflows and
1212	their executions keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
1213	content.
1214	
1215	The response is the updated execution state. Migrating a `completed` or
1216	`terminated` execution returns `409 conflict` and changes nothing. A missing
1217	execution or a target version that does not exist for the workflow returns
1218	`404 not_found`; a cross-tenant reference is the same missing resource. A
1219	missing or mistyped `version`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
1220	`400 validation_error`. Migrating a running execution to the version it is
1221	already bound to returns the current state as-is, appending no event and
1222	writing no checkpoint; a `completed` or `terminated` execution instead
1223	returns `409 conflict` even when the target version is exactly the one it is
1224	bound to. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a `409
1225	conflict`. The migration event is listed directly by the per-execution
1226	events query, and node outputs produced after the migration belong to the
1227	target version's definition. Approver-list validation, lease renewal, and
1228	delivery history keep their existing semantics before and after a migration.
1229	
1230	### Start an execution
1231	
1232	```http
1233	POST /executions
1234	Idempotency-Key: execution-request-1
1235	
1236	{"id":"run-1","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{"order_id":"o-7"}}
1237	```
1238	
1239	Returns HTTP 201. The execution starts in `running` state. Without an
1240	explicit `version`, it binds to the workflow's current version at start time;
1241	naming a `version` binds to that one instead (and a missing version is a
1242	`404 not_found`). See "Workflow versions" for the binding and upgrade rules.
1243	
1244	An execution may declare a timeout:
1245	
1246	```json
1247	{"id":"run-2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{},"timeout_seconds":30}
1248	```
1249	
1250	`timeout_seconds` is a positive number of seconds counted from the moment the
1251	execution starts. Once the deadline passes, the execution terminates with
1252	termination reason `timeout` and no longer accepts output. Executions without
1253	a timeout never expire.
1254	
1255	An execution may also declare its own webhook `subscriptions`, which apply in
1256	addition to the ones its workflow declares:
1257	
1258	```json
1259	{
1260	  "id": "run-3",
1261	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
1262	  "input": {},
1263	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/ops", "events": ["node_completed"], "max_attempts": 3}]
1264	}
1265	```
1266	
1267	### List workflows
1268	
1269	```http
1270	GET /workflows?limit=50
1271	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1272	```
1273	
1274	Enumerates the workflows declared in the request's namespace. The response
1275	is `{"workflows":[{"id":"order-flow"}, ...]}`: one entry per workflow, each
1276	carrying its identifier, in ascending identifier order. A namespace with no
1277	workflows gets the definite empty result `{"workflows":[]}`, not an error.
1278	The query is read-only: it creates nothing, appends no events, and records
1279	no usage, so repeating it returns the same answer and changes no stored
1280	state.
1281	
1282	The list is paged with a keyset cursor:
1283	
1284	- `limit` — required; the maximum number of entries in the page, a positive
1285	  integer. The page never holds more entries than the limit;
1286	- `cursor` — optional; the identifier of the previous page's last entry.
1287	  Only entries whose identifier sorts strictly after the cursor are
1288	  returned, so paging with the previous page's last identifier yields
1289	  consecutive pages that neither overlap nor skip. A cursor past the end
1290	  returns the definite empty list.
1291	
1292	### List executions
1293	
1294	```http
1295	GET /executions?workflow_id=order-flow&status=terminated&termination_reason=timeout&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=run-41&limit=50
1296	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1297	```
1298	
1299	Enumerates the executions in the request's namespace in ascending execution
1300	identifier order. The response is `{"executions":[...]}`; each entry carries
1301	the execution `id`, its `workflow_id`, its `status` (`running`, `completed`,
1302	or `terminated`, always a string), its `termination_reason` (one of the
1303	four termination reasons for a terminated execution, otherwise `null`), and
1304	its `created_at` (the ISO-8601 UTC creation timestamp ending in `Z`), in
1305	that stable key order. A namespace with no executions gets the definite
1306	empty result `{"executions":[]}`. Like the workflows list this query is
1307	read-only and never settles a due timeout, appends an event, writes a
1308	checkpoint, or records usage, so repeated calls return the same answer and
1309	change no state or metering conclusion.
1310	
1311	The same `limit` and `cursor` pagination applies, with the cursor taken
1312	from the previous page's last execution identifier. In addition, five
1313	filters may be combined, and every given filter must match:
1314	
1315	- `workflow_id` — only executions of that workflow. Referencing a workflow
1316	  the namespace does not contain, including one owned by another tenant, is
1317	  the usual `404 not_found` and reveals nothing about its existence;
1318	- `status` — only executions in that lifecycle status. A value other than
1319	  `running`, `completed`, or `terminated` is a `400 validation_error`;
1320	- `termination_reason` — only executions that terminated for exactly that
1321	  reason. The filter is meaningful solely for terminated executions:
1322	  running and completed executions never appear under it, even when other
1323	  filters are given alongside it. An unknown reason is a
1324	  `400 validation_error`;
1325	- `since` and `until` — the same closed creation-time bounds the events and
1326	  metrics queries accept: each is an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp ending in `Z`,
1327	  and an execution whose `created_at` equals `since` or `until` is
1328	  returned. When either parameter is absent the corresponding bound is
1329	  open, so omitting both returns exactly the unfiltered list; a malformed
1330	  timestamp is a `400 validation_error`. When `since` is later than
1331	  `until` the window matches nothing and the result is the definite empty
1332	  list, not an error.
1333	
1334	Both list endpoints follow the usual tenant scope: omitting
1335	`X-Tenant-Id` keeps the single legacy namespace, and a tenant sees only its
1336	own workflows and executions under every combination of filters. Every
1337	parameter may appear at most once; a repeated parameter, an unknown
1338	parameter, a missing `limit`, or a `limit` that is not a positive integer is
1339	a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing.
1340	
1341	### Inspect an execution
1342	
1343	```http
1344	GET /executions/run-1
1345	GET /executions/run-1/events
1346	GET /executions/run-1/checkpoints
1347	```
1348	
1349	The first endpoint returns the materialized state. The second returns the
1350	ordered event stream. The third returns the ordered checkpoints; each entry
1351	gives its `sequence`, the `event_sequence` position it was taken at, the full
1352	`state` summary, and `created_at`.
1353	
1354	The events query is read-only: it appends no events, records no usage, and
1355	changes no state, so advancement, approvals, recovery, and replay never alter
1356	what it observes. With no query parameters it returns the complete ordered
1357	event list exactly as before. It also accepts optional filter and pagination
1358	parameters, which combine as an intersection:
1359	
1360	```http
1361	GET /executions/run-1/events?types=node_completed,node_failed&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
1362	```
1363	
1364	- `types` — a comma-separated set of event types; only events whose type is
1365	  in the set are returned. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown
1366	  event type is a `400 validation_error`;
1367	- `since` and `until` — the same closed-interval occurrence-time bounds the
1368	  metrics query accepts: an event whose time equals either boundary is
1369	  returned. When `since` is later than `until` the window matches nothing and
1370	  the result is an empty list, not an error;
1371	- `cursor` — the sequence of the last event of the previous page; only events
1372	  with a strictly greater sequence are returned;
1373	- `limit` — the maximum number of events in the page, in ascending sequence
1374	  order.
1375	
1376	Every parameter may appear at most once; a repeated parameter, an unknown
1377	parameter, a malformed timestamp, or a cursor or limit that is not a positive
1378	integer is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Filtering never
1379	renumbers events, so paging with `cursor` set to the previous page's last
1380	sequence yields consecutive pages that neither overlap nor skip. A filter
1381	that matches nothing returns the definite empty result `{"events":[]}`, and
1382	querying a missing or another tenant's execution is the usual
1383	`404 not_found`.
1384	
1385	### Webhook notifications
1386	
1387	Subscriptions declared on a workflow or an execution deliver outbound webhook
1388	messages when business events occur. Each webhook subscription contains exactly:
1389	
1390	- `url`: a non-empty `http` or `https` address to POST to;
1391	- `events`: a non-empty array of event types without duplicates, drawn from
1392	  `node_completed`, `execution_completed`, `execution_terminated`, and
1393	  `approval_decided` (a termination is the same event type whatever its
1394	  reason);
1395	- `timeout_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds to wait for each
1396	  delivery attempt, defaulting to 5;
1397	- `max_attempts` (optional): an integer between 1 and 10, defaulting to 1.
1398	
1399	Any other field, a missing `url` or `events`, a mistyped value, an empty or
1400	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
1401	a non-finite number, a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than
1402	ten attempts is a 400 `validation_error` and rejects the whole request — no
1403	workflow, execution, or subscription is partially written. A subscription
1404	may instead declare a queue target (`queue` instead of `url`); see "Queue
1405	subscriptions" below.
1406	
1407	When a subscribed event occurs, a JSON message is POSTed to each matching
1408	target immediately: the body carries `event_type`, `execution_id`, and the
1409	event's details (such as `node_id` for a completed node or `approver` for an
1410	approval decision). Each delivery request carries an `Idempotency-Key`
1411	header; retries of the same event reuse the same key, and different events
1412	never share a key. A delivery is attempted at most the subscription's
1413	`max_attempts` times, with an increasing backoff between attempts. An
1414	unreachable target, a timeout, or a non-2xx response marks the attempt as
1415	failed, but a failed delivery never changes the outcome of the call that
1416	triggered it.
1417	
1418	Deliveries do not append execution events, do not add fields to the execution
1419	state, and are never triggered by replay, recovery, or queries, so
1420	checkpoints and replay conclusions are unaffected. An execution that declares
1421	no subscriptions keeps exactly the same state, event stream, and advancement
1422	results as before.
1423	
1424	### Inspect the delivery history
1425	
1426	```http
1427	GET /executions/run-1/deliveries
1428	```
1429
